title: Past perfect and past simple
subtitle: the present she had given me
summary: Use the past perfect to step back out of a sequence of past events, and know when the past simple is just as good.

lesson.heading: An event out of order
lesson.text: We normally tell a sequence of past events in order, using the past simple. When we need to mention an event *out of order* - one that happened before the last event we spoke about - we can use the past perfect.

examples.text: I **wrote** Clara an email to thank her for the present she **had given** me for my birthday last week.
But as soon as I **pressed** the 'send' button, I **realised** that I **had made** a mistake and sent it to her sister instead.

lesson.note: Order the events happened: gave present - wrote email - made mistake - realised mistake. Order they are mentioned: wrote email - had given present - realised - had made a mistake.

lesson.heading: You don't have to keep it up
lesson.text: Once it is clear that we are talking about events before another past event, we can drop back into the past simple.

examples.text: We bought a new car last month. We**'d driven** my parents' old car for ages, but it **started** to fall apart. We **put** a new engine in it, but that **didn't solve** the problems we were having.
examples.note: or ... had started ... had put ... hadn't solved ...

lesson.heading: When the order is already clear
lesson.text: If time expressions or the context already make the order of events clear, either tense will do.

examples.text: After Ivan **had finished** reading, he put out the light.
The two leaders agreed to meet, even though earlier talks **had failed** to reach an agreement.

lesson.heading: Reporting what was said or thought
rows: I was sure that I **had met** him before. (not ~~I met him~~)
I found that the village **hadn't changed** much. (not ~~the village didn't change~~)
'225 people drowned in the recent floods.'
Police said that 225 people **had drowned** in the recent floods. (or ... drowned ...)
She admitted that she **had stolen** the watch. (or ... stole ...)
lesson.note: A present perfect in the original words has to become a past perfect. An original past simple can stay a past simple.

lesson.heading: Intentions that came to nothing
lesson.text: For things we intended to do but didn't - or won't do now - the past perfect, past simple, past continuous and past perfect continuous are all possible.

examples.text: I **had hoped** to visit the gallery before I left Florence, but it's closed on Mondays.
examples.note: or I hoped ..., I was hoping ..., I had been hoping ...

examples.text: Aron **planned** to retire at 60, but we have persuaded him to stay for a few more years.
examples.note: or Aron had planned ..., was planning ..., had been planning ...

lesson.text: The past perfect is a signal, not a rule: use it when a reader could otherwise get the order of events wrong.

exercises.prompt: As Jonas was introduced to Mrs Lopez, he realised that he ___ her before.
exercises.explanation: His thought was 'I have met her before', and a present perfect becomes a past perfect when reported.

exercises.prompt: I thought it was the best film I ___ in my life.
exercises.explanation: The original thought was 'the best film I've seen', so the report needs the past perfect.

exercises.statement: I found that the village didn't change much.
exercises.explanation: I found that the village hadn't changed much. The original words were 'The village hasn't changed much.'

exercises.prompt: The boy told me that he ___ his train ticket and didn't know how he would get home.
exercises.explanation: Losing the ticket happened before he told me, so the past perfect marks the earlier event.

exercises.statement: The teacher guessed that some of the children had cheated in the exam.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Here the past simple (cheated) would also be possible, because the order is already clear.

exercises.prompt: Match each unfulfilled intention with the way it turned out.

pairs.left: I had hoped to leave by nine,
pairs.right: but I overslept and missed the train.

pairs.left: Lara hadn't intended to become a dentist;
pairs.right: she always wanted to be a vet.

pairs.left: I had expected the operation to be painful,
pairs.right: but I didn't feel a thing.

pairs.left: I hadn't thought of cooking rabbit,
pairs.right: until Andrei told me how tasty it was.

pairs.left: He hadn't meant to insult her,

exercises.prompt: At the conference, scientists reported that they ___ a cure for malaria.
exercises.explanation: The discovery came before the report, so the past perfect keeps the order clear.

exercises.prompt: When I asked Maria about Jakub, she admitted that she ___ from him for ages.
exercises.explanation: Her words were 'I haven't heard from him for ages', so the report uses the past perfect.

exercises.prompt: You overslept and missed the train. Explain what your plan had been.
exercises.answer: I had hoped to leave by nine, but I overslept and missed the train.
exercises.explanation: The past perfect of hope introduces an intention that came to nothing.

exercises.prompt: She said that she ___ her mind who to vote for, and that I couldn't persuade her to change.
exercises.explanation: Her words were 'I've made up my mind', which becomes a past perfect in the report.

exercises.prompt: Julia said she didn't want any dinner. Apparently, she ___ already.
exercises.explanation: Eating came before she spoke, and already points back to the earlier event.

exercises.prompt: In these reports, is the past perfect the only possibility, or would the past simple work too?

items.text: He realised that he had met her before.
He denied that he had taken the money from the office.
I thought it was the best film I had seen in my life.
The teacher guessed that some of the children had cheated in the exam.
She said that she had made up her mind who to vote for.
Thomas explained that he had gone home early because he felt ill.
